docs.title: Welcome
docs.text:
The Checkerboard fMRI Task shows a flickering black-and-white checkerboard on the scanner screen. It is a standard visual stimulus: it switches on and off in blocks, and a dot in the middle gives the participant something to look at. The scanner starts it automatically, so the timing lines up with the scan.

It is a normal Windows program. The scanner PC doesn't need Python or anything else installed.

docs.text:
Download for Windows

This button always opens the newest version. On that page, under Assets, click the file named CheckerboardFmriTaskSetup-v….exe. Then double-click the downloaded file. Getting Started walks you through each step.

docs.title: AI Style Guide
docs.text: A single reference to hand an AI coding assistant — paste it in, or point the assistant at this page — before it touches this codebase. Its job is narrow: keep contributions consistent no matter which human, or which AI tool, produced them, so the codebase doesn't slowly accumulate several different styles and several different toolboxes for the same job.

docs.title: The rule this page exists to enforce
docs.text: Don't introduce a second way of doing something this codebase already does one way. That's Golden Rules's "Pythonic, boring, stock-standard Python" rule, applied specifically to AI-suggested tools, patterns, and dependencies — the place an inconsistent new style is most likely to sneak in unnoticed.

docs.title: Established stack — use what's already here
docs.text:
Job What this project already uses Not: CLI commands click argparse, typer, hand-rolled sys.argv parsing Structured data dataclasses, typing.Protocol contracts plain dicts as pseudo-objects, custom base-class hierarchies Error handling EAFP, specific except tuples broad except Exception, error-code return values Testing pytest unittest as the primary style for new tests, custom test runners Logging stdlib logging print(), a new logging library CLI progress/output rich a second progress-bar or console-formatting library Packaging/versioning setuptools_scm (git tags), PyInstaller hand-maintained version strings, a different bundler

Before adding a new dependency, check requirements.txt first — if something already does the job, use that.

docs.title: Style specifics
docs.text:
• Formatting/linting: ruff — 100-character lines, double-quote strings. Let it format on save; don't hand-format around it.
  • Type hints on every function signature — this is what makes pyright/Pylance catch mistakes at edit time.
  • Naming: snake_case for functions/variables, PascalCase for classes, UPPER_SNAKE_CASE for module-level constants.
  • f-strings for string formatting, not .format() or %.
  • Minimal docstrings — a line or two at most, only where the why isn't obvious from the code itself. Well-named functions and classes do most of the explaining; don't add a docstring that just restates the function name.

docs.title: Patterns to reuse, not reinvent
docs.text:
• EAFP for error handling, with specific exception types named in the except clause — Golden Rules.
  • dataclasses, frozen where the object shouldn't mutate after construction.

docs.title: No flashy new patterns
docs.text:
Specifically avoid, unless there's no working alternative and it's been discussed first: metaclasses, monkey-patching, deeply nested comprehensions or clever one-liners that trade readability for brevity, new decorator-based magic (@deprecated is the one established exception — Golden Rules), and speculative abstractions or config options for a use case that doesn't exist yet — Golden Rules.

If a genuinely better pattern seems worth introducing, propose it explicitly, as its own step, with the tradeoff stated — never slip it in as a side effect of an unrelated change.

docs.title: One file, one step
docs.text: Don't let an assistant touch multiple files, or introduce multiple new patterns, in one proposed change.

docs.title: Teaching examples
docs.text: If an assistant is asked for example code to explain a concept rather than to solve the actual task, keep examples in a clearly separate, obviously fictional domain unrelated to this project's own work (this repo's AGENTS.md, at the workspace root, illustrates this with an everyday domain like library checkouts, bus schedules, or a small inventory — pick whatever fits the concept, but stay in one domain per explanation) — so an example never gets mistaken for, or pasted in as, real production code.

docs.title: Execution exception: code-checking tools
docs.text: AGENTS.md's guardrails otherwise stop an assistant from ever running code itself, requiring every command to be handed to a human to run instead. An AI assistant may run the project's configured checkers — ruff check, ruff format --check, pyright/Pylance — directly. Applying the fixes they suggest is still an edit, and goes through the usual consent gate (or an active BYPASS that covers that file).

docs.title: Execution exception: build scripts
docs.text: An AI assistant may run build.ps1 (Windows) or build_mac.sh (macOS) directly, in any of their modes (-Exe, -Full, -Inno for build.ps1). -Exe/-Full write only into the gitignored build_output/ folder (plus a local editable-install of this same package into the active venv, via pip install -e .) and -Full/-Inno additionally compile the installer with Inno Setup's ISCC.exe, also writing only under build_output/. None of that touches git, a remote system, or any credential. Running the installer .iss script / ISCC.exe on its own, outside of build.ps1 invoking it, is not covered by this exception and still means only suggesting the command.

docs.title: Restricted folders
docs.text: Separate from authorship style: .ai_restricted (repo root, if present) is a human-maintained, .gitignore-style list of folders no AI assistant may read or write — typically example/sample data the user doesn't want an AI touching. Absolute, and not affected by BYPASS — see AGENTS.md's restricted-folders guardrail.

docs.title: Using this page
docs.text: Point any AI assistant here before it looks at anything else in this repo — as a pasted-in reference, or via whatever project config file your tool reads (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, .cursorrules, .github/copilot-instructions.md, …). This repo's own AGENTS.md already does the equivalent for its interaction style; this page is the equivalent for code style and toolbox choices.

docs.title: Development & Building
docs.text: This page is for changing the code. If you only want to run scans, see Getting Started.

docs.title: Set up
docs.text:
You need Python 3.13. A virtual environment ("venv") is a private folder of Python packages for this project only, so it can't clash with anything else on your PC.

py -3.13 -m venv .venv
.\.venv\Scripts\python -m pip install -r requirements.txt -r requirements-dev.txt
.\.venv\Scripts\python -m pip install -e .
.\.venv\Scripts\python -m pytest

The last line runs the tests. If they all pass, you're set up.

docs.title: Run from the venv
docs.text:
pip install -e . adds a checkerboard_fmri_task command to .venv\Scripts\. Activate the venv to use it by name. It reads config\task_config.toml from the repo by default.

.\.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1
checkerboard_fmri_task --check-config   # check the settings
checkerboard_fmri_task --list-screens
checkerboard_fmri_task                  # run a session
checkerboard_fmri_task --config config\test_config_UNVERIFIED.toml

Warning

config/test_config_UNVERIFIED.toml holds best-guess values for trying the software out. Never collect data with it.

docs.title: Where the code lives
docs.text:
Everything is in src/checkerboard_fmri_task/:

File What it does config.py Loads and checks the TOML settings. schedule.py Works out the blocks and flip timing. triggers.py Handles the scanner triggers. timing.py Measures the refresh rate and spots dropped frames. event_log.py Writes the CSV log. checkerboard.py Draws the checkerboard pattern. runner.py Runs a session. Tested with a fake display. presentation.py The only code that uses pyglet (the graphics library). main.py The command line.

Going further

Keeping all pyglet code in presentation.py means everything else can be tested without opening a window. runner.py takes the display as an input, so the tests can pass in a fake one.

docs.title: Build the installer
docs.text:
You need Inno Setup 6 to build the installer.

.\build.ps1 -Full   # exe + installer
.\build.ps1 -Exe    # exe only: build_output\dist\checkerboard_fmri_task\
.\build.ps1 -Inno   # re-make the installer from the last exe build

The installer lands in build_output\installer\.

docs.title: Release a new version
docs.text:
The version number comes from git tags. Pushing a tag that starts with v makes GitHub build the installer and attach it to a new release.

git tag -a v0.2.0 -m "What changed"
git push origin v0.2.0
gh run watch          # follow the build

The download buttons always point at the newest release, so you don't need to change them.

docs.title: Preview these docs
docs.text:
.\.venv\Scripts\mkdocs serve

Then open http://127.0.0.1:8000. Read docrules.md before writing a page.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: This page covers installing the task and running a scan session. You don't need any coding background.

docs.title: 1. Install it
docs.text:
Download for Windows

  1. Click the button above. It opens the newest version's download page.
  2. Under Assets, click the file named CheckerboardFmriTaskSetup-v….exe (for example CheckerboardFmriTaskSetup-v0.1.1.exe). Your browser downloads it.
  3. Double-click the downloaded file and follow the steps.

The installer doesn't need admin rights. It adds two shortcuts to your desktop:

  • Checkerboard fMRI Task starts the task.
  • Checkerboard fMRI Task config opens the settings file, task_config.toml.

\"Windows protected your PC\"

Windows may show this message the first time you run the installer. Click More info, then Run anyway. The installer isn't code-signed (bought from a certificate company), so Windows doesn't recognise it yet. It is the same file built from this project's code.

Updating

To update, run a newer installer over the old one. It saves your old settings next to the new ones as task_config.previous.toml, so compare the two and copy across any values you changed.

docs.title: 2. Check the settings
docs.text: Open the Checkerboard fMRI Task config desktop shortcut. It opens task_config.toml, which holds the timing, the sizes and the number of start triggers to skip. The defaults work, but you should check them against your scan protocol and your projector before collecting data.

docs.title: 3. Check the screen
docs.text:
Run the task's display check on the scanner PC before your first session. Open a terminal (Start → type PowerShell), then copy and paste this line and press Enter:

& "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\Programs\CheckerboardFmriTask\checkerboard_fmri_task.exe" --check-display

It lists every screen with its refresh rate, resolution and Windows scaling. It also shows the checkerboard and fixation sizes in degrees, cm and pixels, and warns you about anything that would stop the stimulus showing correctly.

docs.title: 4. Run a session
docs.text:
1. Start Checkerboard fMRI Task from the desktop.
  2. In the console window, type the participant ID. If the PC has more than one screen, pick the projector.
  3. The task measures the screen's refresh rate (about 2 seconds), then shows the fixation dot and waits.
  4. Start the scanner. The scanner sends a trigger (a Left Shift key press) with each volume. The first few triggers are skipped (dummy_triggers in the settings), and the next one starts the checkerboard.
  5. Press Escape to stop early. The log is saved either way.

docs.title: 5. Find your output
docs.text:
Everything goes to the data folder chosen during install: by default Documents\checkerboard_fmri_task\, opened by the Checkerboard fMRI Task data desktop shortcut. To change it later, set data_dir under [output] in the settings file. The task checks that it can save there right after you enter the participant ID.

If Windows Security's Controlled folder access is on, Windows may block saving to Documents. Allow the program through it, or choose a folder outside Documents (for example D:/fmri_data).

If something unexpected goes wrong, the window stays open with the error, and a crash_<date-time>.txt file is saved in the data folder (the console shows where at launch). Send it to whoever maintains the task.

The data folder holds:

  • sub-<ID>_task-checkerboard_<date-time>_events.csv logs every trigger, block start, checkerboard flip, dropped frame and timing warning. task_time_s counts from the start trigger, and scheduled_task_time_s is when each event should have happened.
  • ..._config.toml is an exact copy of the settings used for that session.

docs.title: All options
docs.text:
Run the program with --help to see every option. Use the same line as in step 3, with --help in place of --check-display.

Option What it does --config Use a different settings file. --participant Set the participant ID without being asked. --screen Pick the screen without being asked. --output-dir Save output somewhere else. --list-screens List the screens and stop. --check-config Check the settings file for mistakes and stop. --check-display Check the screens against the settings and stop (see step 3). --version Show the version and stop. The version is also printed at the top of every run.

docs.title: Golden Rules
docs.text:
A handful of rules of thumb this codebase follows. Worth knowing before you write new code here.

If you're using an AI assistant, also see the AI Style Guide — it turns these rules into a concrete established-stack/avoid-list an assistant can be pointed at directly.

docs.title: Write Pythonic code — don't fight the language
docs.text:
Pythonic means writing code the way Python itself is designed to be written — using the language's own idioms and standard library, instead of patterns carried over wholesale from another language you happen to know better (C-style index loops, Java-style getters/setters). Python has a short, semi-official statement of this philosophy — run import this in any Python shell to see it ("The Zen of Python"). A few lines from it that matter most here: "Readability counts." "Explicit is better than implicit." "There should be one — and preferably only one — obvious way to do it."

Concrete examples, contrasted with the non-Pythonic version scientists coming from another language often reach for first:

# Not Pythonic — manual index loop, a C/Java habit
squared_totals = []
for i in range(len(orders)):
    squared_totals.append(orders[i]["total"] ** 2)

# Pythonic — list comprehension
squared_totals = [order["total"] ** 2 for order in orders]

# Not Pythonic — manual index tracking
i = 0
for order in orders:
    print(i, order)
    i += 1

# Pythonic — enumerate()
for i, order in enumerate(orders):
    print(i, order)

# Not Pythonic — length check standing in for truthiness
if len(kitchen_queue) > 0:
    ...

# Pythonic — empty containers are already falsy
if kitchen_queue:
    ...

# Not Pythonic — manual string building
message = "Order " + str(order_id) + " is " + status

# Pythonic — f-string
message = f"Order {order_id} is {status}"

This project's own EAFP rule below is itself a Pythonic-vs-not example, not a separate idea — try/ except over manual precondition checks is this same principle applied to error handling.

docs.title: Why this matters more, not less, for non-programmers
docs.text:
It's tempting to assume idiomatic Python is a "once you already know Python" nicety, and that someone new to coding is better off writing whatever gets the job done, however verbose. We think the opposite:

  • Every beginner-facing Python resource teaches the idiomatic way. Tutorials, official docs, and Stack Overflow answers all model list comprehensions, with blocks, f-strings, and so on. Code that goes against the grain cuts you off from being able to look up your way through a problem — the answer you find won't look like the code in front of you.
  • Non-Pythonic code carried over from another language brings that language's bugs with it. Manual index loops are exactly where off-by-one errors live; if len(x) > 0 and if x quietly diverge the moment x turns out to be None instead of just empty.
  • It's what the rest of this codebase already looks like. Reading Pythonic code elsewhere in this project and then writing non-Pythonic code yourself doubles the number of styles you have to hold in your head at once — code that reads like what you write is part of what makes a codebase learnable in the first place.

docs.title: Prefer boring, stock-standard Python
docs.text:
Related but distinct: even within idiomatic Python, prefer the plain, well-known feature over the clever or exotic one. Standard library over a dependency that reinvents it; a straightforward function over a metaclass or decorator trick doing the same job less legibly; pathlib.Path over hand-rolled string path-joining.

Reasons this earns its place as a rule, not just a stylistic preference:

  • Boring code fails predictably. When something breaks in a script built from stock for loops and if statements, the error is usually exactly where it looks like it is. Clever code — deeply nested comprehensions, __getattr__ magic, monkey-patching — can make the actual failure point invisible.
  • Debuggable by more people. Someone a few months into Python can step through boring code and understand every line. That's not true of code leaning on rarely-used corners of the language — which, in a lab where people rotate through every few years, is exactly the code most likely to get quietly abandoned rather than fixed.
  • It ages well. Flashy patterns tend to be trend-driven; basic control flow and the standard library have stayed the same for two decades and will likely outlast whichever clever technique looked good this year.

docs.title: Always use Path, never strings, for files and folders
docs.text:
Every folder or file passed through this codebase — a CLI argument, a filename handed between functions — should be a pathlib.Path, never a bare str. This is narrower than the general "prefer pathlib.Path" point above: it's a hard rule for this specific case, not just a style preference.

# Not this — string in, string out, joined by hand
def find_participant_file(data_folder: str, participant_id: str) -> str:
    return os.path.join(data_folder, f"{participant_id}.csv")


# This — Path in, Path out
def find_participant_file(data_folder: Path, participant_id: str) -> Path:
    return data_folder / f"{participant_id}.csv"
  • String path-building is where platform-separator bugs come from — str(a_path).split("_") silently breaks on Windows because str() renders backslashes that a string-oriented split doesn't expect. Use .name, .stem, .parts, or / instead of manual string splitting/joining, and the platform's separator is never something your code has to reason about.
  • CLI entry points should hand back Path from the start, via click.Path(..., path_type=Path), rather than a plain string that gets wrapped in Path(...) partway through the function.

docs.title: Ask forgiveness, not permission (EAFP)
docs.text:
Python has a strong, named idiom for how to handle things that might go wrong: EAFP — "Easier to Ask Forgiveness than Permission." The idea: just try the thing, and handle the specific exception if it fails, rather than checking every precondition first and only proceeding if they all pass (that alternative style has its own name too: LBYL, "Look Before You Leap").

# LBYL — check permission first
if item_type in self.items:
    return self.items[item_type]
else:
    raise ValueError(f"Store has no item of type {item_type.__name__}")

# EAFP — ask forgiveness instead
try:
    return self.items[item_type]
except KeyError as e:
    raise ValueError(f"Store has no item of type {item_type.__name__}") from e

Both versions do the same thing here, but EAFP is the more idiomatic — and often faster — Python style: the "normal" path stays uncluttered by precondition checks, and the failure handling lives in one place (the except block) instead of being scattered through if/else branches.

That only works well combined with the next rule, though — EAFP still needs the except to name specific exceptions, not swallow everything.

docs.title: Catch specific exceptions, not broad ones
docs.text:
Every except block names exact exception types, e.g.:

except (ValueError, FileNotFoundError) as e:
    ...

never a bare except: or except Exception:. A broad except doesn't fix a bug — it hides the symptom, and quietly swallows any other unrelated error of the same type too.

The rule: if you're tempted to widen an except tuple to make an error go away, that's usually a sign you need an explicit guard (if x is None: ...) instead — not a broader except.

docs.title: Write code for today, not for a hypothetical future
docs.text:
Do not rewrite everything at once. Preserve working behaviour and improve one structural issue at a time.

In practice: don't add configuration options, abstractions, or flexibility for a use case that doesn't exist yet. If a genuine second use case shows up later, that's when the abstraction earns its keep.

docs.title: Mark old code @deprecated — don't just delete it or leave it silently
docs.text:
When code is superseded but not yet safe to delete (e.g. other code still calls it, or you want a record of why it was replaced), mark it with typing_extensions.deprecated instead of quietly leaving it in place or removing it outright:

from typing_extensions import deprecated

@deprecated("Superseded by match_intervals(); kept until callers migrate")
def old_match_intervals(...):
    ...

The decorator doesn't stop the function from running; it makes type checkers (like pyright) flag any call site with a warning, showing your message as the reason. That gives anyone still calling it — including future-you — an explicit, visible reason to migrate, instead of the function just quietly rotting or vanishing without a trace.
